lignes.texte: For decades, we’ve been told the U.S. military is the most expensive machine on Earth.
But in fiscal year 2024, that changed.
For the first time in history, the U.S. government spent about $882 billion just
on net interest, surpassing the $826 billion spent on national defense.
The Pentagon was overtaken by the cost of interest on its own debt.
And that started a ticking clock… one that most people still aren’t paying attention to.
Meet Mark.
He lives in Columbus, Ohio and works in logistics for a mid-sized manufacturing company.
Every April, he pays his taxes without much thought, like most Americans. In his mind, that
money is supposed to turn into something solid. Roads. Schools. A military that keeps the country
stable. The basics of a functioning nation. The national debt always felt distant. It’s
the kind of thing politicians argue about on TV, not something that touches his day to day life.
$35.7 trillion is just a number to him. Too large to picture, too disconnected to feel
real. It’s like trying to count every grain of sand on a beach or every star in the sky.
It wasn’t his grandparents’ problem. It wasn’t his parents’ problem.
So why would it be his? Except it is.
What Mark doesn’t know is that the U.S. government collected roughly $4.9 trillion in tax revenue
in fiscal year 2024. It spent $6.8 trillion that same year. Nearly $2 trillion was borrowed money.
That’s nothing new.
It’s a tale as old as time for prosperous post-war America. What is new is where the money is going.
For decades the biggest line items in the federal budget were all pretty
predictable. Social Security, Medicare, defense. The things a country buys when
it’s trying to take care of its people and protect its borders.
But in 2024, a new entry muscled its way to the top of the ledger book: The cost of borrowing
money that was already spent. The interest on the national
debt hit a cool $882 billion. Just 2 years earlier, it was only
the seventh largest line item in the federal budget. By 2024, it had surged to second place,
overtaking Medicare, overtaking defense, and now sitting behind only Social Security.
And that interest was ballooning at such an alarming rate it made
every other line item look like a rounding error.
Up 34% in a single year.
America has always been about pushing new frontiers. Well, here’s one it never
wanted to cross. In 2026, interest payments will cross the $1 trillion mark for the first time.
It won’t stop there.
Over the next decade, the U.S. government is projected to spend
$16.2 trillion on interest alone. That's nearly double what it spent
in interest over the previous two decades adjusted for inflation.
Think about what that amount of debt means in human terms. It’s enough to give every
single one of the 3.2 million public school teachers in America a $4 million
raise. It’s basically enough to wipe out all outstanding student loan debt 9 times over.
Instead, all of it just…vanishes.
It produces nothing, builds nothing, and goes directly to bondholders that
own them. Bondholders being the official term for a gaggle of foreign governments,
domestic banks, pension funds and the like.
That’s the price the United States government must pay.
And the trajectory is unlike anything the country has seen since World War II. Back in 2024,
publicly held debt was sitting pretty at 98% of the entire U.S. economy. Today, it has surpassed
it. And by 2047, that number is projected to reach 200% of the entire U.S. economy.
The country’s debt will be growing more than twice as fast as the economy.
Every year that passes, the financial hole deepens faster than growth can close it.
Five years ago the average interest rate on the national debt was 1.84%.
Today it’s hovering north of 3.3% and climbing fast. Older low-rate debt is
expiring and getting refinanced at whatever the market demands.
Think of it like a mortgage that never fully gets paid off. The
government finances itself by selling bonds,
basically IOUs to investors around the world. Short-term, long-term, all at different rates.
Right now, the government’s longest-term IOU, a 30-year bond, is yielding 5.19%,
its highest level in 19 years. That matters because it sets the price of
new borrowing. Every time older, cheaper debt rolls off, it gets replaced at the
higher rate. The system starts putting more expensive debt on top of the old.
The blended average keeps ratcheting up, and economists have calculated the breaking point.
If that average hits around 6.3%, a level the U.S. has
paid before,interest alone would eat up every dollar collected in federal taxes.
Every dollar Mark sends to Washington in April, used to pay off the debt’s weighty interest bill.
We’re not there yet. But consider where we already are. 18.5 cents
of every federal dollar collected in 2025 went straight to interest,
which was already a record set above the previous high in 1991.
By 2036, under current projections, that figure will hit nearly 26 cents.
One in four dollars spent just keeping the debt from collapsing under its own weight.

Mark doesn’t feel any of this yet. His paycheck always looks the same, and the roads in Columbus
always feel like they’re generally improving. The news cycles spout the same old thing.
But somewhere between the spreadsheets and the auction houses and bond markets,
something irrevocably bad has already broken. Mark had a flight booked for a trip he’d been
looking forward to for months. Nothing exotic, just a long weekend in Tampa to see his college
roommate. He booked it on Spirit Airlines because it was cheap, and it got him there in one piece.
He’d flown Spirit more times than he could count. Cramped seats, no extras, nothing fancy,
but it worked. It showed up, it took off, and it landed where it was supposed to.
The week before his trip, Mark opened his email and saw one unread message.
Spirit Airlines was shutting down immediately. After 34 years in the air, the airline was gone.
Just like that, Mark became one of tens of thousands of passengers stranded mid-booking.
Flights were canceled and plans erased. Thousands of Spirit Airline employees were suddenly out in
the cold seeking work elsewhere. Hoping for an eventual refund,
Mark had to scramble for a last-minute ticket on Delta that cost him three times as much.
He figured it was a one-off. People had seen the writing on the wall for Spirit.
Bad management, maybe? Bad luck?
Nope.
Turns out it was neither. And Spirit wasn’t alone.
What happened to Spirit was happening across the country, and it was happening at Mark’s
manufacturing company too. His company wasn’t growing. Raises had been frozen
for the third year running. The new equipment his boss promised last spring never showed up.
There was talk of restructuring. Nobody has been fired yet. But nobody was being hired,
either. The whole place felt like it’s running in place.
Mark assumes it's just the economy. There’s always rough patches in his industry,
and things should pick up soon. This time, though, they won’t. Because Mark’s company,
like Spirit and thousands like it are already dead in the water.
They just don’t know it yet.
For much of the past decade interest rates were at historic lows. Borrowing money was almost free.
So companies like Mark’s that weren’t especially profitable would keep themselves alive by taking
out cheap loans to cover the gap, pay their bills, service their old debt, and pay their employees.
Economists have a name for these companies. They call them zombie firms. Their achilles
heel isn’t anything dramatic, just their fundamental, recurring need to
borrow to keep themselves afloat. And there are thousands of them operating in the U.S. alone,
These companies stumble forward on cheap debt the way a person survives on credit
cards after losing their job. It’s a way of biding their time. They’re so buried in debt
they can’t even cover the interest payments on their loans from what they actually earn.
Sound familiar?
You may have heard of some of them. JetBlue. Peloton. Wayfair. Bed Bath & Beyond. Household
names, all of them, but ones kept breathing by an IV drip-feed of cheap borrowed money.
The part that would really make Mark’s stomach drop is how the company chose to survive.
A huge chunk of its debt wasn’t used to build better products or improve their service. It
was used to buy back its own stock and make the company look healthier on paper than it actually
was. In extreme cases, it was used to inflate executives’ pay packages. At Bed Bath & Beyond,
the top three executives collected $140 million in compensation while the company
spent $7 billion on stock buybacks. Then it went bankrupt. Tens of
thousands of workers lost their jobs. The executives, of course, kept the money.
The reckoning arrived fast when interest rates rose and all the
cheap money dried up. Business bankruptcies jumped 22% in 2024
alone, the third straight year of increases after a decade of decline.
One investor who famously predicted the last two market crashes warned that worse lay ahead.
He said it was “objectively the greatest tinderbox-timebomb in financial history,”
one where a single wildfire could burn the economy far worse than the Great Depression.
Zombie firms are notorious for doing more than just hurting shareholders when they finally
collapse. While they’re alive, they act like a slow drain on the economy. They tie up workers,
office space, equipment, and credit that could be flowing to healthier, growing companies instead.
So when a scrappy startup with a genuinely useful product can’t get a loan because
banks are already loaded up with zombie debt. Wheninnovation slows, or when wages stop rising,
that’s when people like Mark start to feel it. The whole economy starts moving in slow motion.
America has always assumed it was immune to this kind of slow-motion decay. Other
countries have too. Look no further than Japan, a country that once had a world-class economy,
cutting-edge industry, and absolute confidence in its own exceptionalism.
In 1989, Japan was the envy of the world. Its companies were buying up American landmarks,
and its banks were the largest on Earth. Japanese land was worth more than anything,
ever. At its peak, the land itself underneath the Emperor’s palace in central Tokyo was estimated to
be worth more than every piece of real estate in the entire state of California combined.
Then, it all popped.
The Nikkei stock index started a steady skid downward, losing almost 40% of its
value in a single year. It kept tanking for 2 more, eventually losing nearly two-thirds
of its peak value. Businesses were failing at astonishing rates. Even though no single company
collapsed overnight, by the end, the country with the second-largest economy on Earth simply
stopped growing. An entire generation grew up not knowing what economic momentum even felt like.
From 1995 to 2025, Japan's share of the entire world economy shrank
from 17.8% to 3.6%. Japanese workers couldn’t afford homes. They delayed
marriage. Birthrates soon collapsed, and many withdrew from society entirely.
They coined a term for these people: Hikikomori. People so ground down by
decades of economic stagnation they simply stopped playing the game.
The United States thinks it’s different.
But it’s entering a critical phase of its financial history with a few
things Japan didn’t have at the start of its lost decade. A national debt already
humming along at 100% of its GDP with an interest bill growing faster than
the economy itself and 2,000 zombie companies hollowing out the workforce.
And in Washington, the government might be about to discover it has a zombie problem of its own.
By 2030, Mark has started paying attention to the news in a way he never used to. He has to. Grocery
prices keep jumping. The mortgage refinance quote he got was high enough to make his stomach turn.
At a family barbecue in Columbus, he brings it up. His brother-in-law shrugs.
“Doesn’t matter. We’re America. The whole world uses our money. They’ll keep buying our debt.”
Mark wants to believe that. It’s comforting. The idea that no matter how bad things get,
the rest of the world is contractually obligated,
in some unspoken way, to keep bailing out the U.S. Deep down, he knows that deal is falling apart.
For 80 years, being the world's reserve currency was America's superpower. To buy oil,
trade with each other, or keep one’s vaults as a safety net, every country on earth needed
dollars. And the easiest way to hold onto dollars safely was to buy U.S. government
debt. It was the deal of the century. America could borrow almost unlimited amounts of money,
at incredibly low rates, because the entire planet needed somewhere to
park its cash. U.S. Treasury bonds were considered the safest asset on Earth.
Economists call this phenomenon the “exorbitant privilege,” a phrase
coined decades ago by a French finance minister speaking out of pure jealousy.
Everyone knows privileges can be revoked.
In October 2025, something happened that had not happened in about 30 years.
For the first time since the late 1990s, the physical gold reserves sitting in the world’s
central banks became worth more than all the U.S. Treasury bonds they were holding combined.
This is the central point for these central banks: It did not take long for them to start
trusting their own gold bars rather than the portions of the U.S. government debt they held.
Poland, India, Turkey, China, and dozens of others have started to move their money out
of American IOUs and into something the U.S. can’t print, freeze, or sanction.
In the last few years alone, central banks bought more than a thousand tons of gold per year,
year-over-year. China has slashed its U.S. Treasury holdings from a
peak of $1.3 trillion in 2013 down to under $700 billion, the lowest share it’s held since 2001.
Why?
Because in 2022, when the U.S. and its allies froze hundreds of billions of dollars belonging
to Russia’s central bank overnight. The rest of the world got the message loud and clear. If you
make America angry, you can lose access to your own money, no questions asked, no warning given.
So, the slow exit began.
Emphasis on slow, since you can’t just dump trillions of dollars in
U.S. debt overnight without crashing the value of what you’re holding. It’s
more like watching water find its way out of a cracked dam.
It’s slow and methodical until it isn’t, all at once.
Here’s what it means for Mark. The U.S. government needs to borrow roughly $2
trillion every single year just to cover the gap between what it spends and what it collects.
For decades, foreign buyers were a massive, reliable chunk of the customers showing up
to buy that debt. Now, as they choose to buy less while demanding more in return,
someone else has to step in and fill the gap.
That someone is America.
For a few years, the Federal Reserve actually tried to do the opposite. It pulled back from
the bond market, hoping the rest of the world and domestic investors could absorb the difference.
By the end of 2025, the number didn’t add up. The Fed announced
it had to reverse course entirely and start buying U.S. debt again,
essentially printing new money to cover what foreign buyers would not.
When the buyer pool shrinks and the amount of debt for sale keeps growing,
there’s only one way to attract the buyers who are left: Pay them more.
Higher rates mean the government has to spend more money just paying interest. To
cover that bigger bill, it borrows even more. And the more it borrows, the more
lenders start asking to be paid for the risk. Before long, the problem starts feeding itself.
Mark doesn't know any of that. He just knows his mortgage rate
is higher than anything his parents ever dealt with. And he's starting to
think his brother-in-law's explanation wasn't much of an explanation at all.
But the scary part isn't the debt. It's what happens when
the debt starts changing everyone else's behavior. It’s 2033. Mark is 44 now. His kids are in middle
school, and he’s started doing the things people in their 40s do.. checking retirement calculators,
wondering if he’s behind, wondering whether Social Security will still be around when he needs it.
For most of his life, that question felt almost ridiculous. Of course it would be there. It had
always been there. His grandparents got checks. His parents got checks. Social Security was
just part of the furniture. It was one of those government programs that worked in the background.
Then his phone starts blowing up. The Social Security trust fund which has been topping
up monthly checks for retirees for decades is running dry. Imminently.
The trustees who manage the program have moved up
the date so many times it's started to feel like a countdown clock that
only ever ticks one direction. The latest projection today is insolvency by 2032.
When that actually happens, the law doesn't allow the government to just print extra checks to cover
the gap. The payments will automatically shrink with a 22% across-the-board cut, to everyone.
Overnight.
For the average retiree, that's about $500 less every single month,
forever, unless something changes.
There’s another turning point in 2033, one far beyond the confines of Social Security.
For decades the federal government collected tax revenue and used it to pay for everything
its citizens needed. There was always a gap between revenue and spending. That’s the
deficit. But that gap was manageable, a bill you could put on the credit card and chip away at.
By 2033, that bill becomes the entire budget.
There’s nothing left, not a penny. Everything you need to fund the military, NASA, the FBI,
national parks, food safety inspections,
air traffic control, and disaster relief has to come from somewhere else entirely.
And that somewhere else… is borrowing.
It’s the moment economists call the fiscal event horizon.
Before, the government could borrow for things like stimulus, upgrades or crisis
response. But this is different. Now it has to run a deficit just to keep the basics going,
the non-negotiable stuff that holds the country together.
After that, there’s a choice to be made with no good options. Either you slash Social Security
and Medicare further, well past the 22% cut that’s already coming. Which is a political death knell.
No politician survives being the one who cut Grandma’s check on purpose.
Option two is to print more money. Have the Federal Reserve buy up the debt the rest of
the world won't, creating new dollars out of thin air to cover the gap. This doesn't require
anyone to vote for anything painful. But the pain eventually shows up for everyone, all at once.
Mark doesn’t know it yet, but his government is about to choose option two.
Mark used to think there were only two endings to this story. Either
the government just keeps borrowing forever and everything somehow keeps running. Or,
one day the bill comes due, the money runs out,
and the United States declares bankruptcy. Neither of these things happen.
People can go bankrupt. Companies can go bankrupt. The United States cannot go bankrupt.
Why?
Because when people borrow money, we borrow in a currency we don't control.
For example, if you take out a loan in dollars,
you have to go earn dollars to pay it back. And if you can't, the bank takes your stuff.
But the U.S. government borrows in dollars. And the U.S. government
is the only entity on Earth legally allowed to create more dollars. It is,
quite literally, the house that owns the printing press the casino runs on.
So when the bill comes due - and by 2034, that bill will be absolutely enormous - the
Federal Reserve has an escape-hatch option no ordinary borrower has.
It can simply create the money to pay for it. Creating more money doesn’t create more real
things. It doesn’t build extra houses, produce more cars, or put additional
groceries on the shelves. The actual supply of goods and services stays the same.
What changes is the number of dollars trying to buy them.
And when more dollars are chasing the same amount of things, each dollar buys a little
less. Prices adjust. Slowly at first, then all at once in ways people notice in everyday life.
This is the default. It just doesn’t look like one yet.
When America actually defaults, there won’t be any press conferences announcing what just happened.
The government will still pay every bill, on time, in full, exactly as promised. Grandma will still
get her social security check. And the dollar amounts will be correct, right down to the cent.
Those dollars just don’t buy what they used to.
This already happened to Mark once, and he barely noticed it at the time. Between 2020 and 2025,
prices in America rose by roughly 25%, more than double the rate of the 5 years before that.
If you took the $10,000 Mark had sitting in a savings account in early 2020,
you’d know he didn't spend a dime of it. He just left it there, the way you're supposed
to. But by 2025, that same $10,000 could only buy what about $7,500 used to buy.
$2,500 dollars worth of value, shaved clean off the top in the span of just 5 years.
You can imagine that process at a much larger scale. It’s the only tool left
in 2034 that doesn’t require a single politician to vote for anything painful.
It’s exactly what economists mean when they talk about the debt getting
“inflated away.” The government will still pay you back in full,
but the dollars you earned for your retirement account will not grow faster than prices rise.
It’s a form of tax, but not one you signed up for.
It’s the only tax in American history that collects itself.
It’s 2038, and Mark is approaching 50. His kids are grown. His daughter
finished college four years ago, and she’s still living at home.
Not because she isn’t trying. Rent in any city with decent jobs
eats more than half of an entry level paycheck. Buying a home feels like something from another
era. It’s something people inherit, not earn. She’s been with her boyfriend for 6 years,
but there’s no engagement, no wedding plans. Mark stopped asking a while ago.
Mark doesn’t know it, but the story he’s living is the story of Japan,
30 years later, with an American accent. In Tokyo in the 1990s, a generation of
young people did everything they were told to do. They got educated, they showed up,
they looked for stable jobs. They tried to build the same kind of life their parents had.
Instead, they ran into something they couldn’t really see coming.
An economy that had stopped making room for them. Moving back in with their parents indefinitely
was a form of economic and social adaptation. Delaying marriage was a hallmark of demographic
evolution. There was just never enough money to get around to it. By 2020,
27% of Japanese women reached age 50 without ever having had a child. It was the highest
rate among developed countries, and more than double what it was just fifteen years earlier.
Multiply that pattern across an entire population, for an entire generation,
and it becomes its own kind of crisis. If nothing changes,
Japan's population is projected to shrink from 125 million people to around 87 million
by 2070. Spiraling birth rates. Hikikomori are withdrawing from society altogether.
This is what economists mean when they talk about “Japanification.”
It’s what happens when countries with decades of stagnant growth lose their long-term stability.
By 2038, Mark’s daughter isn’t fighting it anymore. What’s the point of organizing
or protesting in the streets for change? She’ll just continue to wait for rent to
become affordable again, for wages to catch up. For some version of the future her father had.
She doesn’t know she’s living inside a case study. The only thing she knows is that every year,
the gap between the life she was promised and the life she's living gets a little wider.
And nobody in charge seems to be in a hurry to close it.
From her point of view, the American Dream hasn’t died, but it does feel deferred. And
when you defer something long enough, it starts to look exactly the same as dead.
Now stop the clock. Rewind everything. Go back to today.
The interest bill hasn’t surpassed the military budget. The fiscal event
horizon is still just an ominous forecast of dark clouds on your local news station.
The truth is that every single thing we mentioned is still technically avoidable. It isn’t fate,
it’s a trajectory. And those can be changed by people willing to grab ahold of the wheel.
But the word “willing” is doing an awful lot in that
sentence. The fixes aren’t secret or complicated.
They’re just brutally unpopular.
Fixing this mess means closing the gap between what the government spends and
what it collects years before the 2032 Social Security cliff,
not after. That means choices most people don’t want to talk about. Raising the retirement age
as lifespans increase. Means-testing benefits so the wealthiest retirees get less. Reworking
how benefits are calculated so the system holds together long-term instead of being
patched year to year. None of it is painless.
All of it is just trying to make the math work again before time does it for us.
It also means dealing with the zombie problem head-on. Letting genuinely unviable companies fail
instead of propping them up with cheap credit. That would free up capital and workers for the
businesses that are actually building the future. And it means, eventually, an honest conversation
nobody in Washington wants to have. The bill for the past 30 years has to be paid by someone. The
longer it’s delayed, the more it falls on people like Mark, and you, and me. It is,
in the most literal sense, a thankless job. The benefits will accrue to future generations,
but the blame goes to whoever's in the room when the hard votes happen.
That’s the real crisis if America can’t start getting its debt under control. It isn’t the
debt itself. The crisis is a system where everyone can see the problem, everyone agrees it’s real,
and yet no one in a position to fix it has any real incentive to act before the damage lands.
Until then, it’ll continue the same way it has for the past 30 years. Interest compounding on
interest. Promises compounding on promises. Until one day, the bill arrives at a door near you.
People like Mark didn’t build this system. They just inherited it.
The question is whether his kids will too.
If this broke your brain a little, wait until you see what’s happening to the
housing market. Or the job market. Or your retirement account. Watch The American Dream
Is Dead. Millennials Are OBLITERATED to see how it all connects. Or click on this video.
